k: Home About About Heritage Spices Rooted in Idukki. Built for global kitchens. Heritage Spices is an export business built around one ingredient we care deeply about: green cardamom from the hills of Idukki, Kerala. Our story Cardamom is often called the queen of spices, and Kerala’s Idukki district is one of the places it has long been grown. We started Heritage Spices to bring that harvest to buyers who care about where their ingredients begin, and who want a supplier that communicates clearly. We work directly with farmers in Idukki, and we select pods carefully for colour, aroma and condition before they are prepared for export. Our focus today is on importers, wholesalers and food and beverage businesses in the Gulf, where cardamom is part of everyday hospitality. What we stand for 01 A traceable origin We source directly from growers in Idukki, so we can talk about where your cardamom came from and who grew it. 02 Careful selection Pods are chosen for a clean aroma, even colour and good condition, because small differences are easy to taste. 03 Clear communication Written specifications, samples before orders, and straight answers on availability, packing and paperwork. Where our cardamom grows Idukki sits in the Western Ghats, a cool, humid, rainy landscape that suits cardamom. Plants grow under tall shade trees, and pods are picked by hand in rounds as they ripen. You can read more in our journal note on why Idukki cardamom has a character of its own . Who we work with We talk to spice importers and wholesalers, coffee and tea blenders, bakeries and sweet makers, and food manufacturers. If you buy for the UAE , Saudi Arabia , Qatar , Kuwait , Oman or Bahrain , we would be glad to hear from you. Buyers from other countries are welcome to get in touch too. Working

t: Cardamom in Arabic Coffee: Why the Pod Matters
d: Why green cardamom is at the heart of Gulf coffee, and what coffee blenders and importers should look for in a pod.
k: Home Journal Cardamom in Arabic coffee: why the pod matters Gulf traditions · 4 min read Cardamom in Arabic coffee: why the pod matters Why green cardamom is at the heart of Gulf coffee, and what coffee blenders and importers should look for in a pod. Across the Gulf, coffee is more than a drink. Serving Arabic coffee, often called qahwa or gahwa, is a gesture of welcome, and cardamom is what gives it much of its recognisable fragrance. Saudi, Emirati, Qatari, Kuwaiti, Omani and Bahraini versions differ in roast, colour and extra spices, but cardamom is a constant across them. Why green cardamom Arabic coffee is usually lightly roasted and brewed with ground or crushed cardamom, sometimes alongside saffron, cloves or other spices. Because the coffee is delicate, the cardamom is easy to taste. A pod that smells musty or flat will show up in the cup, while a fresh, sweet and clean pod lifts the whole drink. What blenders and importers look for People who blend or trade cardamom for coffee tend to focus on a few things. They look for a bright, even green colour, which usually points to careful picking and drying. They want a strong, sweet aroma when a pod is cracked open, and uniform size so that a blend behaves the same each time. Cleanliness matters too: whole pods with few splits, stalks or dust are easier to grind and pack. Whole pods keep their aroma Cardamom holds its fragrance best inside the pod. Once seeds are removed or ground, the aroma tends to fade faster, so many buyers prefer to buy whole green pods and process them close to the time of use. Whole pods also make it easier to check quality by eye and nose before you buy. t: Green Cardamom Sizes Explained: A Buyer’s Guide
d: A plain-language guide to how green cardamom is sized and why size, colour and uniformity all matter in a specification.
k: Home Journal Green cardamom sizes explained: what buyers should know Buyer guide · 3 min read Green cardamom sizes explained: what buyers should know A plain-language guide to how green cardamom is sized and why size, colour and uniformity all matter in a specification. When you buy green cardamom in bulk, size is one of the first things on the specification. It affects how the pods look, how they are priced and sometimes how they are used. Here is a simple way to think about it. How size is described Pod size is commonly expressed in millimetres, for example 6 mm, 7 mm or 8 mm and above, with larger pods often described as bolder. Different suppliers and markets use different grading names, so the clearest approach is to state the size you want in millimetres in your enquiry, and to approve a sample against it. Size is not the whole story A large pod is not automatically a better one. Colour, aroma, moisture and cleanliness all matter. Some buyers, such as coffee blenders, may care most about aroma and uniformity, while retail packers may care more about the look of the pod on the shelf. Uniformity helps repeat orders If you plan to buy again and again, uniformity is as important as the size itself. A lot with pods of similar size, shape and colour is easier to pack, easier to describe to your customers and easier to reorder consistently. How to specify your order In your first message, mention the size you prefer, the colour and aroma you expect, the packing you want and the country you are shipping to. You can send all of this on our sample request page . We will confirm what is currently available and send a sample for approval. For more background, see what to look for in a premium green pod . Importing cardamom from India is straightforward when both sides are clear from the start. This checklist covers the points that most often decide whether a first order goes smoothly. Rules differ by country and can change, so always confirm the latest requirements with your clearing agent. 1. Write your specification Describe what you need: size in millimetres, colour, aroma, moisture expectations, packing size and the market you will sell into. Even a few lines give both sides something to check against. 2. Approve a sample first Ask for a sample and compare it with your specification. Agree what the sample represents and what you will approve before anything ships. 3. Choose your delivery terms Common terms are FOB, where the supplier loads the goods at the Indian port and you arrange the freight, CFR, where the supplier pays the freight to your destination port, and CIF, which adds insurance. Pick the one that suits how you already work with freight forwarders. 4. Check packing and labelling Confirm packing sizes and what must appear on the label. Several Gulf markets have their own labelling expectations, including language requirements, so check with your agent before you finalise. 5. Prepare the documents Shipments usually involve a commercial invoice, a packing list, a bill of lading or airway bill and a certificate of origin, plus any other certificates your destination requires. t: Why Idukki Cardamom Has a Character of Its Own
d: How hills, shade, rain and careful hand harvesting shape the aroma of cardamom from the Western Ghats.
k: Home Journal Why Idukki cardamom has a character of its own Field notes · Idukki · 3 min read Why Idukki cardamom has a character of its own How hills, shade, rain and careful hand harvesting shape the aroma of cardamom from the Western Ghats. Cardamom is a plant of the forest understory. It grows best on cool, humid, shaded hillsides with steady rainfall, which describes much of the Western Ghats in Kerala. Idukki district sits in the middle of that landscape and is closely tied to the story of Indian cardamom. The surrounding region is often called the Cardamom Hills. Hills, shade and rain Elevation, regular rain and filtered light all influence how a cardamom plant grows and how its pods develop. Plantations in Idukki are commonly laid out beneath taller shade trees, which keeps the plants cool and protects the soil. Many are managed at a small scale, often by families who know their land closely. A harvest that comes in rounds Cardamom pods do not ripen all at once. A plant flowers and fruits over an extended period, so pickers return to the same plants several times in a season and choose pods at the right stage of maturity by hand. Picking at the right moment matters because it affects colour, aroma and how well a pod holds its character after drying. Why origin matters to a buyer For a buyer, origin is more than a place name. Knowing where a pod was grown, and who grew it, makes it easier to talk about consistency, to trace a lot, and to understand why one harvest smells and tastes the way it does. That is the idea behind Heritage Spices: staying close to the farmers of Idukki and keeping the conversation clear from the first sample to the final shipment. t: What to Look for in Premium Green Cardamom Pods
d: A simple checklist for judging colour, size, aroma and consistency in green cardamom.
k: Home Journal What to look for in a premium green pod Buyer guide · 3 min read What to look for in a premium green pod A simple checklist for judging colour, size, aroma and consistency in green cardamom. Green cardamom is judged first with the eyes and the nose. Specifications and lab tests matter too, but an experienced buyer can learn a great deal from a handful of pods on a table. Colour Good green cardamom is known for a bright, even green. Pods that look pale, patchy or bleached can point to uneven drying or long storage. Colour is not the only measure of quality, but it is often the first thing a buyer notices. Size and uniformity Pods are usually graded by size, and size is often discussed alongside price and intended use. Just as important is uniformity: a lot where the pods are similar in size, shape and colour is easier to work with and easier to repeat from one shipment to the next. See our guide to green cardamom sizes . Aroma Break a pod or crush a few seeds and smell them. The aroma should be fresh, sweet and clean. Musty, flat or dusty notes suggest moisture or old stock. Condition and cleanliness Look for whole pods with few splits, stalks or foreign matter. Moisture control matters, because pods that are too damp can deteriorate in storage and in transit. Ask for a sample The best way to judge any lot is to see it. Ask for a sample , compare it with your own specification, and talk through the points that matter for your market, such as grade, packing and how the cardamom will be used. t: Clearer Spice Supply Chain Conversations
d: Practical points that help importers and exporters agree on specifications, samples and paperwork early.
k: Home Journal Building clearer conversations across the supply chain Export conversations · 3 min read Building clearer conversations across the supply chain Practical points that help importers and exporters agree on specifications, samples and paperwork early. Most problems in the spice trade are not caused by the spice. They come from a gap between what the buyer imagined and what the supplier understood. Clear conversations at the start prevent most of them. Start with the specification Describe the product you need in plain terms: grade or size, colour, moisture expectations, packing and the market it is for. A written specification gives both sides something to check against. Agree on samples Samples are the common language of the trade. Agree what the sample represents, how it was drawn from the lot, and what the buyer will approve before anything ships. Raise paperwork early Documents and requirements differ by destination country. Buyers should share any import rules, testing or labelling needs at the start, and suppliers should confirm what they can provide, so there are no surprises close to the shipping date. Keep communication simple Quick, direct answers, a single point of contact and honest updates on harvest and availability go a long way.
